title: Time to Heal-ey
gist: Resolution Foundation's weekly note tots up the first week of Andy Burnham's premiership: a 5 per cent VAT cut on energy bills, a GBP 2 bus fare cap and pub business rate cuts worth over GBP 67 a year to a typical family but costing over GBP 2 billion in 2029-30, cutting fiscal headroom to around GBP 8 billion and leaving Chancellor John Healey to find money at the Budget or reverse the energy VAT cut. It also flags research showing Germany's short-time work scheme merely postponed adjustment, that municipal debt by 1900 was almost as large as the corporate bond market with no local authority defaults, and that facially 'masculine' leaders correlate with institutional decline and militarised conflict.

insights.claim: The largest measure in the new UK government's first week was a 5 per cent VAT cut on energy bills, accompanied by a GBP 2 bus fare cap, together worth over GBP 67 of support a year to a typical family.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A small per-household transfer with a large aggregate price tag -- energy suppliers and bus operators see revenue effects while the fiscal cost lands on the Budget.
insights.locator: The biggest by far was the 5% VAT cut on energy bills

insights.claim: Including business rate cuts for pubs, announcements from a single week carry a total cost of over GBP 2 billion in 2029-30, taking the estimated fiscal headroom down to around GBP 8 billion.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: GBP 8 billion of headroom is thin enough that a single forecast downgrade forces tax rises -- the key number for gilt and sterling risk into the Budget.
insights.locator: Alongside the business rate cuts for pubs

insights.claim: The binary facing the Chancellor is explicit: either John Healey finds more money in the Budget, or he puts energy bills back up by 5 per cent -- because the funding detail is flimsy and it is ambiguous whether the measures are permanent.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A dated, falsifiable fork at the Budget -- a reversal would be an inflation-positive surprise, while funding it implies departmental cuts or tax rises.
insights.quote: either John Healey needs to find more money in the Budget, or he needs to put up energy bills back up by 5%
insights.locator: The funding debate has focused on both the flimsy detail

insights.claim: The open question is whether the week's funding signals indicate a broader willingness to cut departmental spending to put money back in people's pockets, or merely the opening skirmishes of a government yet to face the big trade-offs.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Frames the strategic read for UK fiscal positioning: a transfer-over-services government would imply persistent pressure on public sector suppliers.
insights.locator: Stepping back, what’s most interesting to me

insights.claim: There is analytical value in a government visibly trying even when global events determine outcomes -- a tactic Luke Tryl was optimistic about on the Foundation's podcast.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Suggests political durability may hold up even if the cost-of-living measures fail economically -- relevant to handicapping UK policy continuity.
insights.locator: On our latest podcast episode Luke Tryl was optimistic

themes.theme: Short-time work schemes postpone rather than avoid adjustment

insights.claim: Germany's permanent short-time work scheme, which allows flexible reduction in hours with partial wage subsidies for hours not worked and was loosened through the pandemic, cost GBP 45 billion between 2020 and 2021.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A benchmark cost for labour-hoarding policy that European governments will revisit in the next downturn.

insights.claim: Firms taking up the German short-time work scheme during Covid were disproportionately weaker performers on productivity and quality measures, but this selection pattern did not hold during the financial crisis -- so the nature of the shock determines whether such schemes support viable or zombie firms.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Shock-dependence means job-retention schemes cannot be evaluated generically; in demand shocks they may preserve productivity laggards and suppress reallocation.
insights.locator: The paper finds that firms taking up the scheme during Covid

insights.claim: Scheme-using German firms saw employment run 3-4 per cent higher than non-users, but the effect evaporated fast once firms left the scheme -- reality was postponed, not avoided.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Implies deferred layoff waves rather than saved jobs -- a template for reading labour market data after any subsidy scheme unwinds.
insights.locator: The same firms saw employment run 3-4 per cent higher

insights.claim: College-educated men who face greater local marriage-market competition work longer hours and earn more, apparently to make themselves more attractive marriage prospects, according to research using a competition index built from marriage patterns of 18-45-year-olds and local population data.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A non-obvious driver of hours worked and earnings dispersion -- demographic sex ratios as an input to local labour supply forecasts.

insights.claim: Among non-college-educated women, greater marriage-market competition increases the likelihood of dropping out of the official labour force entirely, while non-degree men work fewer hours largely because they become less likely to work at all.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Adds a social-demographic channel to the UK and US inactivity puzzle that pure economic models miss.
insights.quote: Unromantic as it sounds, the dating market and labour market remain tightly intertwined.

insights.claim: By 1900, English municipal debt was almost as large as the corporate bond market and around half the size of the national debt, having grown from London's sewage-infrastructure issuance to fund streets, trams and schools.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A historical existence proof that a large sterling sub-sovereign bond market is possible -- directly relevant to fiscal devolution proposals under Burnham.

insights.claim: Almost all 19th century English municipal borrowing came from private lenders rather than Whitehall, and not a single local authority went bust.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A zero-default track record is the strongest argument fiscal devolutionists have; watch for it in any UK council bond market revival.
insights.locator: Almost all of it came from private lenders

insights.claim: The caveat on municipal borrowing is that all borrowing has to be repaid by someone in the end, whether it is a war bond or a local bond -- devolved debt does not create fiscal capacity, it relocates it.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: Tempering note for anyone treating devolved borrowing powers as new headroom rather than relabelled liability.
insights.locator: though we mustn’t forget all borrowing has to be repaid

insights.claim: Research mapping the facial width-to-height ratios of over 2,000 world leaders across 184 countries and more than 150 years -- using the ratio as a biological marker for testosterone-driven behaviour -- finds leader masculinity has increased over the past 70 years, with spikes during geopolitical turbulence such as the Cold War.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: A quantified secular trend in leader selection that correlates with geopolitical stress cycles -- an unconventional lens on political risk.

insights.claim: More masculine-faced leaders were found to be much more likely to preside over institutional decline and to engage in militarised conflict.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: If the correlation holds, leader-selection trends are a leading indicator for conflict risk and institutional quality -- worth noting even at low conviction.
insights.locator: The authors also found masculine leaders

themes.theme: Council housing arithmetic (chart of the week)

insights.claim: The new Social and Affordable Homes programme has a GBP 39 billion envelope targeting 300,000 affordable homes with a full 60 per cent earmarked for social rent, positioning it as the vehicle for Burnham's council housebuilding ambition.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: The existing programme already carries most of the stated ambition -- limits how much genuinely new supply the political pledge implies.

insights.claim: The tenure trade-off is stark: hold the money fixed and chase 100 per cent social rent and you build 50,000 fewer homes overall; hold the homes fixed and you need GBP 8 billion more in grant, because social rent brings in less lifetime rental income and needs a bigger upfront grant to stack up for a housing association.
insights.speaker: @resfoundation
insights.so_what: The clean either/or that any council housing announcement must resolve -- watch which side of it the Budget lands on.
insights.quote: Because bricks don’t care about tenure, but the Treasury does.
insights.locator: So why not go the full hog
